cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Can't tell — Longitudinal ten-year qualitative case study; no information is reported on interview refusals, non-response, or participant withdrawal.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable — Qualitative anthropological case study with no statistical effect estimation; competing hydrogeological, financial, political, and anti-development explanations for municipal decisions are explored narratively.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate — Identifies specific local legal and administrative instruments governing piped water access (RE-3 rural estate minimum lot-size zoning of 0.8 ha vs. 2.0 ha, Agricultural Land Reserve status, Official Community Plan subdivision limits, Bylaw No. 1410 granting sole discretion over connection sizing/location to the municipal engineer, local-improvement petition thresholds of 50% of properties representing two-thirds of assessed land value, and the 6th edition Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality), though bylaws are summarized from secondary municipal records rather than analyzed doctrinally verbatim.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern — Multi-source documentary and transcript triangulation strengthens reconstruction of public events, but interview guides/procedures are unreported and physical water-quality and quantity evidence relies on conflicting secondary consultant and health-board reports sampled at differing times and well locations.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak to Moderate (secondary/contested) — Institutional outcomes (council motions, committee recommendations, and the August 2007 CAD $1.6M infrastructure grant) and household coping behaviours are well documented via public records, whereas drinking-water contamination and yield metrics derive from small, non-standardized secondary well surveys (7–8 wells among 64 households) and anecdotal well logs.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern — Stakeholder claims and archival excerpts are synthesized narratively without a transparent coding matrix, and an unedited chronological contradiction appears between Section 4.4 (PDF p. 7, reporting January 2007 council approval and August 2007 grant funding) and Section 7 (PDF p. 9, stating that at the time of writing council decided not to support the watermain extension).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell — Documentary compilation appears comprehensive across municipal minutes, consultant reports, and local press, but purposive sampling and recruitment criteria for the 22 stakeholder and resident interviews are not reported, preventing verification of balance across opposing factions.

domain_ratings.justification: The author clearly states the goal of explicating the decade-long conflict over extending a municipal watermain by 4 km to 64 well-dependent properties on Senanus Drive in Central Saanich, British Columbia, and formulates two explicit research questions regarding how municipal engineers evaluate contradictory safety evidence and integrate diverse forms of knowledge.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF Page 1) and Section 1 Introduction (PDF Pages 1–2)

domain_ratings.justification: An anthropological science-and-technology-studies (STS) qualitative approach is well suited to examining how competing technical reports, resident lived experiences, municipal politics, and land-use policies interact in contested public-works decision-making.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1 Introduction and Section 2 Method (PDF Pages 1–2)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Research design appropriate to address aims
domain_ratings.justification: A longitudinal ten-year single-case field and archival design—tracing actors, public hearings, task-force deliberations, and engineering memoranda across the life of the controversy and contextualized by two related multi-year community studies—appropriately addresses the research aims.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF Page 1) and Section 2 Method (PDF Page 2)

domain_ratings.justification: Although 22 interviews were conducted with major players and residents (including the mayor and chair of the water and waste management committee), the paper gives no explanation of how interviewees were identified, selected, or invited, what proportion of pro- versus anti-watermain residents or engineering staff participated, or whether any approached individuals declined.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Data collected in a way that addressed research issue
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection combined extensive documentary archives (newspaper articles, municipal and regional minutes, Giles/CHR/Lowen water reports, WATF majority and minority reports, well logs, personal notes), audio recordings/transcripts of public meetings (including the 22 September 1999 open house and public hearing), and 22 interviews, directly capturing the epistemic and political conflict, although interview topic guides and interview recording procedures are not specified.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Method (PDF Page 2), Section 5 (PDF Page 7), and Reference 17 (PDF Page 10)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered (reflexivity)
domain_ratings.justification: The author states a Latourian commitment to symmetry—withholding personal opinions to present stakeholder interpretations—and notes conducting two other multi-year studies in the same watershed/community, but does not critically examine his own relationship with local actors, potential influence in a small community, or how researcher positionality shaped data collection and selection.

While Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada grant support (#410–99–0021) is acknowledged, the paper reports no institutional ethics review, informed consent process for the 22 interviews or personal notes used, or confidentiality safeguards in a named municipality with identifiable public officials and task-force chairs.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Method (PDF Page 2) and Acknowledgements (PDF Page 10)

domain_ratings.justification: The Method section states that multiple data sources were triangulated, verified, or presented as conflicting, and three students are thanked for data-collection assistance, yet no systematic qualitative coding procedure, analytical audit trail, or team verification process is described; moreover, an unresolved internal discrepancy exists between Section 4.4 (PDF p. 7, documenting 2007 approval and CAD $1.6M grant funding) and Section 7 (PDF p. 9, asserting that at the time of writing council decided not to support the watermain extension).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Method (PDF Page 2), Section 4.4 (PDF Page 7), Section 7 (PDF Page 9), and Acknowledgements (PDF Page 10)

domain_ratings.justification: Empirical findings regarding the clash between competing hydrogeological/health assessments, anti-development municipal politics, petition/cost-allocation barriers, and the mediating predicament of municipal engineers are clearly articulated and supported by multi-perspective documentary evidence, notwithstanding the minor unedited timeline discrepancy in Section 7.

domain_ratings.domain_name: How valuable is the research (narrative assessment)
domain_ratings.justification: High substantive value for understanding the municipal legal and administrative last mile: the case vividly demonstrates how local zoning rules (RE-3 minimum lot sizes), local-improvement petition thresholds, council anti-sprawl politics, and contested water-quality testing protocols blocked piped water extension to 64 contaminated/low-yield well properties for decades, and proposes structured decision-support frameworks (Bayesian networks and Ecopath ecosystem modelling) to integrate local testimonial and technical evidence.

overall_narrative_summary: Roth (2008) presents a ten-year qualitative anthropological case study of the struggle by 64 well-dependent households on Senanus Drive (Central Saanich, British Columbia, Canada) to obtain a 4 km municipal watermain extension. Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study exhibits clear aims, an appropriate longitudinal ethnographic/STS case-study design, rich multi-source documentary and meeting-transcript triangulation, and clear substantive findings on how municipal bylaws (RE-3 zoning, Bylaw No. 1410, petition thresholds), anti-development politics, and conflicting groundwater reports constrained safe-water access (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q5, Q9 = Yes). However, methodological reporting shows moderate concerns across four items (Q4, Q6, Q7, Q8 = Can't tell): interviewee sampling and recruitment for the 22 interviews are unspecified, researcher-participant reflexivity in a long-studied local community goes beyond a generic neutrality claim without self-critique, research ethics and consent/anonymity procedures are omitted, qualitative coding mechanics are not detailed, and an unedited manuscript contradiction appears between Section 4.4 (reporting 2007 council support and CAD $1.6M tripartite grant funding) and Section 7 (stating that at the time of writing council decided not to support the extension). Overall methodological concern is Moderate (4 Can't tell items out of Q1–Q9).
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (4 Can't tell items out of Q1-Q9)
study_design_identified: Anthropological / ethnographic qualitative case study (22 stakeholder/resident interviews, public meeting audio recordings/transcripts, and longitudinal documentary triangulation)
where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Section 1 Introduction (PDF Pages 1–2); Section 2 Method (PDF Page 2); Section 3 Background and context (PDF Pages 2–4); Section 4 Senanus Drive case history, water-quality reports, municipal engineering issues, and 2007 funding outcome (PDF Pages 4–7); Section 5 Conflicting interests and politics (PDF Pages 7–8); Section 6 Municipal engineers' role (PDF Page 8); Section 7 Conclusions and conceptual Bayesian/Ecopath recommendations (PDF Pages 8–10); Acknowledgements and References (PDF Page 10).
why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical design (Section 2 Method, PDF p. 2) is a ten-year anthropological qualitative case study drawing on 22 interviews, audio recordings of public meetings, and archival/documentary triangulation. Quantitative groundwater levels and coliform/chemical figures in Sections 3–4 are secondary extracts from pre-existing municipal/consultant reports analyzed qualitatively as contested knowledge claims rather than primary quantitative data collection by the author, and Section 7 proposes purely conceptual Bayesian/Ecopath frameworks. Thus, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the exact matching tool rather than MMAT, ROBINS-I, or NONE.
